newsitem.title: USA: Eli Lilly says Q4 Prozac sales up 17 pct.
newsitem.headline: Eli Lilly says Q4 Prozac sales up 17 pct.

text.p: Eli Lilly and Co, reporting higher 1996 fourth quarter results, said Monday that Prozac sales rose 17 percent to $603 million in the quarter.

The increase in Prozac sales came on strong U.S. sales, offseting lower non-U.S. sales due to "continuing competition from generic forms of Prozac in Canada and Australia and substantial competitive pressures in France," Lilly said.
"Growth comparisons for Prozac in the quarter were positively affected by U.S. wholesaler purchasing patterns in both 1995 and 1996," the company said.
Shares in the drugmaker were off one to 81-7/8.

For all of 1996, worldwide sales of the anti-depressant were $2.356 billion, an increase of 14 percent from 1995. U.S. sales were up 20 percent, while international sales were essentially flat, Lilly said.
Zyprexa, a treatment for schizophrenia launched in the 1996 fourth quarter, had sales totaling $86.9 million after three months on the market.
"Zyprexa is already marketed in 11 countries throughout the world, with several additional launches expected to take place in the near future," Lilly said.
Gemzar, launched in the United States in May as a treatment for pancreatic cancer, had sales of $26.3 million for the fourth quarter and $61.9 million for the year.
ReoPro, a blood clot buster, had fourth-quarter sales of $50.8 million and year sales of $149.3 million.

Investment in research and development increased 23 percent in the quatter, to $349.4 million from $284.5 million a year earlier, "primarily due to expenses in support of clinical trials and development expenditures for products, such as raloxifene, that are in the later and most expensive phases of clinical research," Lilly said.
For the year, spending in research and development increased 14 percent, Lilly said.

The fourth-quarter effective tax rate was 22.7 percent, compared with a fourth-quarter 1995 rate of 14.4 percent, Lilly said. "Fourth-quarter comparisons of income from continuing operations were negatively affected by the significantly different tax rates," Lilly said.

"The 1995 tax rate was adjusted downward in the fourth quarter to recognize increased volume of products and earnings in countries where tax rates are lower and to recognize the effectiveness of various tax strategies," it said.
"The effective tax rate for the full year of 1996 was 25 percent, compared to 26 percent in 1995," Lilly said.
Lilly posted 1996 income from continuing operations of $1.523 billion, or $2.78 per share, up from $1.307 billion, or $2.30 per share, excluding discontinued operations, a year earlier.

"In addition to the three percent growth in operating income, income from continuing operations benefited from a lower effective tax rate and a significant increase in other income realized through previously disclosed nonrecurring transactions," Lilly said.

Earnings-per-share calculations for the year also benefited from a reduction in the number of shares outstanding as a result of the Guidant Corp split-off, completed in September 1995, the company said.
Lilly sales for 1996 rose nine percent, to $7.347 billion from $6.764 billion in 1995. Volume increased 11 percent.
Exchange rates and selling prices each reduced sales by one percent, Lilly said.
Worldwide pharmaceutical sales and services for the year grew nine percent, to $6.787 billion from $6.242 billion in 1995.
Total U.S. pharmaceutical sales and services increased 12 percent from 1995, Lilly said.
"International pharmaceutical sales were up four percent with volume growth of 10 percent, which was largely offset by unfavorable exchange rates and a reduction in selling prices," the company said.
Sales of the human insulin Humulin rose 12 percent for the fourth quarter to $238.6 million. For the year, global sales of Humulin were $883.9 million, up 11 percent from 1995.
Worldwide sales of animal health products increased 13 percent for the fourth quarter and seven percent for the year, "with growth principally occurring in international markets," Lilly said.
